posts.content:
Every B2B PR team I've worked with can tell you their impression count from last quarter. Not one of them could tell you if it moved a deal.

That question is never "how many people saw it." It's "what did it change."
The gap between those two answers is where PR budgets die. Not because the work didn't perform. Because the person holding the budget couldn't connect coverage to anything they're measured on. Impressions don't show up in a board deck next to pipeline and revenue. So PR gets framed as discretionary spend.

The fix isn't perfect attribution. Perfect attribution doesn't exist in Communications. It barely exists anywhere in marketing right now. The fix is choosing what you're going to measure before the campaign launches, not scrambling to justify it after.

Three frameworks I keep coming back to: tying earned media value to LTV:CAC, running pre/post lift measurement around major placements, and tracking direct plus AI-sourced traffic increases after coverage hits. None of this requires new tooling. It requires a different starting point.

The PR teams with the most internal influence aren't the ones with the best coverage. They're the ones whose CFO can explain, in their own words, what the PR program drove last quarter.

If your CFO can't do that today, the coverage isn't the problem.

posts.content:
Your north star metric is either building your business or quietly killing it. The metric your marketing team celebrates every week might be the exact reason your CFO is asking hard questions in QBR.

Most SaaS teams default to MQLs because they're easy to count and easy to celebrate. What they're not is financially meaningful. 

Your CFO doesn't build a revenue model around MQL volume. Your board doesn't evaluate growth efficiency by lead count.

NSM selection starts with one question...what metric, if it moves, guarantees the business is growing? 

For most SaaS companies that lives in one of two buckets. 

1️⃣ Growth efficiency: CAC, LTV, payback period. 

2️⃣ Qualified pipeline: demos booked, total SQLs, LTV:CAC ratio, win rate.

Pick the one that reflects where your business actually is. 

Early stage with poor unit economics own CAC and payback period. 

Established with a pipeline coverage problem own SQLs and win rate.

The metric you choose determines what your team builds toward. Get that wrong and everything downstream is optimized for the wrong outcome.

What's your current NSM and does your whole GTM team actually know it? ⬇️

posts.content:
Every B2B ecommerce brand that comes to us from a DTC agency tells us the same thing about their old agency. They were optimizing for more traffic and clicks. In B2B e-comm, that's the wrong goal entirely.

More traffic doesn't mean more revenue when your buyer is a procurement manager comparing specs, not an impulse shopper checking out in two minutes. 

The conversation has to start somewhere else entirely.

Before touching a single channel, the question is: what's the holistic strategy? Then it's channel by channel. Is Google Shopping optimized for the way B2B buyers actually search?

Is Amazon protected from the resellers undercutting your price on your own listing? Is MAP being enforced, or is your pricing strategy quietly falling apart across channels nobody's watching?

DTC agencies don't ask these questions because DTC doesn't have these problems. They've never had to think about a reseller eating margin on their own product, or a channel conflict that could cost a distributor relationship.

We took the targeting discipline we built in B2B SaaS and applied it to commerce. The result is the same buyer logic, whether someone's buying a CRM or a projector for a school district.

That's the gap DTC agencies can't close. We built Commerce specifically to close it.

posts.content:
Your catalog has thousands of SKUs. The buyer searching for your exact product right now can't find a single one.

Industrial B2B buyers don't search like consumers. They're not browsing. They already know what they need. A specific part number, a voltage rating, a thread pitch, a material grade. 

That search string is essentially a purchase order. The only question is whether your catalog shows up when it happens.

Most don't. Not because the products aren't there, but because the product data isn't built for how B2B buyers actually search.

Catalog completeness for industrial brands means a few specific things. 

✅ MPN capture in every title. 
✅ Spec-based naming...not "industrial valve" but the exact voltage, thread pitch, and material grade in the title itself. 
✅ Product data structured the way Amazon Business and Google Shopping actually rank and surface results, not the way it looks clean in your internal system.

The gap between those two things is where your highest-intent buyers disappear.

How is your team currently handling catalog structure for B2B search? ⬇️

posts.content:
The B2B brands that lose to AI commerce won't know it's happening until it's too late. It starts with a broken feed. Here's why.

Buyers used to open seven tabs to research a purchase. Specs, pricing, supplier reputation, distributor comparisons. It took time. That's why B2B marketing was always hard to prove, because the research cycle was long and invisible.

That cycle is collapsing.

Buyers are now opening a chat window, brain-dumping exactly what they need, and asking AI to tell them who to buy from. The research still happens. The buyer just outsourced it to a machine.

And that machine has zero patience for incomplete data.

Missing product titles. 

Broken product pages. 

Feeds without specs or part numbers. 

These were always problems that cost you conversions. They are now problems that cost you the consideration set entirely. AI will not cite you, recommend you, or surface you. 

It moves on to the brand whose catalog it can actually read.

The brands that win agentic commerce are not the ones with the best products. They are the ones with the cleanest, most complete, most machine-readable catalog data. 

That is a feed problem. That is a structured data problem. That is exactly what Lauren Marks and Directive Commerce is built to solve.

Fix the feed now or lose to a competitor who did.

Ask ChatGPT who the best vendor in your category is. If your name doesn't come up, ChatGPT doesn't know who you are and neither does your buyer.

ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini don't pull vendor recommendations out of thin air. They surface what's already structured, credible, and confirmed across the web. 

If you don't know what shapes that, you can't influence it.

A few things actually move the needle here. 

Consistent entity information across your website, LinkedIn, and third-party sites. AI engines cross-reference for confirmation, so conflicting descriptions of what you do hurt you.
 
Earned media and third-party mentions matter more than your own website copy, because AI engines weigh external validation heavily. 

Structured, specific language about who you serve and what problem you solve beats vague positioning every time, because there's nothing concrete for the model to latch onto.

Most brands are still optimizing for keyword rankings while their buyers are getting answers from a model that's reading something completely different. 

This isn't a checklist you finish once. It's an ongoing presence you maintain, the same way you'd treat SEO five years ago.

If you're not sure how your brand shows up when someone asks an LLM the question that matters to your business, that's worth finding out before you find out the hard way.

posts.content:
Nobody cares about your firm's positioning statement other than your marketing team. And the reason why may surprise you.

Most positioning statements get built the same way. A workshop, a whiteboard, a list of adjectives, and a vote on which ones "feel right." 

Experienced. Innovative. Client-first. Whatever wins gets put on the website and called differentiation.

Nobody outside that room ever believed it, because it was never sourced from anything real.
A positioning statement isn't supposed to be chosen. It's supposed to be sourced. It should come from what your founders and execs actually believe about the market, the problem, and why your approach is right.
 
If that belief doesn't already exist inside the people running the company, no amount of wordsmithing creates it.

And belief that isn't said out loud doesn't count as positioning. It's just an opinion nobody's heard.

This is why executive thought leadership isn't a nice-to-have next to your positioning. It's the mechanism that makes positioning real. 

A founder who says the same thing consistently, in public, with conviction, is proof the positioning statement is true. A founder who never says anything is proof it was never more than copy.

Your buyers can tell the difference. Can your execs?

Amazon is discounting your products below MAP right now. And there's nothing in your distributor agreement that stops it.

The most consequential decision most industrial manufacturers haven't made consciously is 1P vs 3P. Getting it wrong is expensive in ways that don't show up until the margin is already gone.

1P means Vendor Central. Amazon buys your inventory wholesale, controls your retail pricing, and can discount whenever they want. You get distribution. You lose margin control.

3P means Seller Central. You own pricing, content, and the buyer relationship. Higher operational lift, but brands that migrate successfully are documenting margin improvements of 20 to 56% on the same catalog volume.

The right answer depends on your current channel architecture, where margin is bleeding, and what your distributor agreements actually allow. That's the audit that has to happen before anyone touches a campaign.

Most manufacturers skip straight to optimization. The infrastructure decision comes first.

If you're an industrial brand trying to figure out the right path forward, talk to Lauren Marks at Directive Commerce. ⬇️
